activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
story:
Georgia stood at the folding table outside the fire station with a stack of the Riverside Beacon, the school paper she edited, and nobody would take one. Voters hurried past her with their stickers on, heads down, and the man at the door kept glancing her way like she was trouble waiting to happen.

"Excuse me," he finally said, crossing the parking lot. "You can't hand those out here." He tapped the headline, which read SCHOOL BUDGET CUTS: WHO DECIDES? "This is a polling place. It's volatile enough without kids pushing opinions at people."

"It's not an opinion," Georgia said. "It's reporting. And it's the November issue, not election stuff." Her social studies assignment was due Monday: pick a right from the Bill of Rights and explain it in her own words. She had planned to write about the Fifth, because it sounded mysterious, like something from a courtroom show. Now she wished she had read further down the page.

"You seem like a smart kid," the man said, softening his tone but not his position. "Let's compromise. Move across the street and you can hand out as many as you want."

Georgia picked up the stack anyway. "Who says I have to move? Newspapers are protected in the United States. It's in the First Amendment." She had memorized the sentence in class without really hearing it, but standing there with forty unread papers, she heard it now. "The First Amendment to the Constitution protects freedom of religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly and petitioning the government. The press. That's me."

The man crossed his arms. "The Constitution doesn't let you block a doorway."

"Then I'll stand by the bike rack. That's not blocking anything." She carried the stack over and set it on the rack, then held one paper up like a menu. An older woman in a red coat slowed down, took a copy, and started reading before she even reached her car. Then a man in coveralls took two. Within ten minutes, seven papers were gone, and nobody had shouted or shoved, which seemed to surprise the man at the door as much as it surprised Georgia.

He walked over, slowly, hands in his pockets. "My daughter wanted to start a paper at her school," he said. "The principal shut it down last spring. I told her it was probably for the best." He looked at the remaining stack, then at the voters drifting past with copies tucked under their arms. "I may owe her a phone call tonight."

"You could also take one," Georgia said. "For context." She held out the last paper, and he took it, folded it carefully, and put it inside his jacket like something worth keeping.

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
story:
Ariana had the notes. She knew the twelve-bar progression cold, could pound out the chords with her eyes shut, and yet every time she tried a solo in the music room after school, it came out sounding like a robot reading a grocery list. Marcus, who played bass in their little trio, flopped backward on the piano bench beside her and groaned.

"Those are the right notes," he said. "I checked. So why does it sound like a vending machine reciting poetry?"

"Maybe I'm just a negligent pianist," Ariana said, poking one key with dramatic shame. "Guilty of musician negligence."

"You're not negligent, you're stiff," said Priya from behind the drum kit. "Everything's even. Dum, dum, dum, dum. Like a metronome with no imagination."

Ariana frowned at her hands. Something tugged at her memory, back to the fall, when her grandmother had put on an old record and shuffled around the kitchen in her slippers while the piano on the recording swung so hard it seemed to wink. Ariana had tried to tap along and kept landing in between the beats, and her grandmother had laughed and said, "That's the shuffle rhythm, honey, each pair of eighth notes is played long-short instead of evenly." Ariana had thought it was just something grandmothers said. Now she sat up so fast she nearly knocked the sheet music off the rack.

"Long-short," she muttered. "Not even. Long-short." She played two eighth notes, the first stretched and the second clipped, then two more, then stitched them into a little line. The music room instantly felt warmer, like the sun had come through the blinds on purpose.

"Wait," Marcus said, sitting up. "Do that again."

She did it again, and this time she climbed the progression with it, letting the long notes lean and the short ones scamper after. Priya caught the feel within a bar and lightened her hi-hat to match, and Marcus's bass started walking like it had somewhere fun to be. Ariana took a breath and assessed her options for the turnaround, chose the bent third everyone loves, and hung on it just long enough to make Marcus grin like a consumer who'd just found the last cookie in the package.

"Now it's blues," Priya said. "Before, it was homework."

"One more time," Ariana said, "and this time I'm going all the way up to the turnaround and jumping off." Her left hand landed on the first chord, long-short, long-short, and the room began to swing.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
story:
Gate B14 smelled like burnt coffee and pretzels, and the departure board said DELAYED in the same cheerful red letters it probably used for everything. Florence unpacked her science homework on the seat beside her: two printed climate graphs, one for the Sonoran Desert and one for the Amazon rainforest, and a worksheet that wanted a comparison of rainfall and temperature. Her little brother, Milo, was supposed to be watching the window for their plane, which mostly meant breathing on the glass.

She looked at the desert graph first. Along the bottom ran the months, January to December. There was a zigzagging line that climbed in summer and dropped in winter, and there were short bars along the bottom of the chart too. Florence frowned. Which one was temperature? The bars went up and down a little, and she'd assumed, back at home, that taller bars meant hotter months. But some of the tallish bars sat under the winter part of the line, where it sagged low, and that made no sense at all. Deserts were hot all year, weren't they?

"Your plane's not coming," Milo reported, without turning around. "Neither is anybody's."

Florence ignored him and studied the rainforest sheet. Same setup: months along the bottom, a line, and bars. Here the bars were enormous, towering columns in every single month, while the line stayed almost flat near the top of the chart. If the bars were temperature, the rainforest would be boiling in every month of the year and the desert barely warm at all. That was backwards. She tried to formulate another idea and got nowhere for a minute, because both ideas seemed wrong.

Then she flipped the sheets side by side on the plastic armrest. The line on the rainforest graph sat high and flat; the line on the desert graph went up and down like a yo-yo. The bars did the opposite, huge in the rainforest and tiny stubs in the desert. So the line had to be the temperature, and the bars had to be something the rainforest had plenty of and the desert had almost none. She checked the tiny numbers on the left and right edges of the chart and confirmed it, feeling like she'd found a secret door in a wall she'd been staring at for an hour. The bars were rainfall, the line was temperature, both on the same chart, month by month.

"Rain," she said out loud.

"What?"

"Nothing. Homework." It had been tedious until it wasn't. She picked up her pencil and started writing: the desert's temperature swings wildly while its rainfall bars stay almost invisible, and the rainforest's line stays steady while its bars tower over everything. A woman across the aisle peered over, saw the two graphs, and gave Florence a nod of deep respect, or possibly pity.

"Flight 447, now boarding," the speaker crackled. Milo was already gone, dragging his backpack toward the line.

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
story:
Cole's little sister had drunk half of a suspicious glass of lemonade before announcing that it tasted "weird and zingy," and now Cole needed to know whether Grandpa had mixed up the sugar with something else. The kitchen counter was lined with supplies from Grandpa's old chemistry box: a roll of paper strips, a chart with colors from red to purple to blue, and a note in faded pencil. Grandpa was out in the garden, so Cole was on his own.

He tore off a strip and dipped it into the lemonade. The paper turned red, fast, like it had been waiting for this. He checked the chart. Red meant acid. Lemonade was supposed to be a little acidic anyway, wasn't it? He stared at the glass, trying to reason about a thing he couldn't see. Something invisible was in that drink, and the paper was the only witness willing to talk.

Then he tested plain water, and the strip refused to commit, staying purple-ish, and he remembered the word from the chart: neutral. He tried milk, which edged toward blue, the direction the chart called basic. So the paper could tell him a hidden property of any liquid. That meant he could compare. He dipped a fresh strip into the lemonade again and held it beside the milk strip and the water strip, side by side on a white plate. The lemonade strip was redder than anything a normal glass of lemonade should manage. Something extra was in there.

He carried the plate outside, squinting in the sun like the strip was a laser pointer he could aim at the truth, but sunlight didn't help. Grandpa was kneeling by the garden wall, and Cole noticed the crusty gray-green patches growing on the rocks, the kind that looked like paint someone had dripped and abandoned. "Grandpa, what's that stuff on the wall?" he asked, mostly to delay telling him about the lemonade.

"That's lichen," Grandpa said. "Funny you ask. Those strips you're using, the litmus paper, it's made from that. Litmus is a dye they get out of lichens." Cole looked from the wall to the plate in his hands. The paper that had turned red came from the crusty growths on the rocks. He felt like he'd been let in on a secret the kitchen had been keeping.

"About the lemonade," he started, and Grandpa's eyebrows went up before Cole even finished the sentence. They walked inside together, Grandpa sniffed the glass, and after one cautious sip he set it down and looked at Cole. "That," he said, "is my pickle brine." Cole's sister appeared in the doorway, licking her lips. "Can I have more?"

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
story:
Lucy stood in front of a glass case in the history museum, staring at a small leather book with cracked binding. Her class assignment was due Monday: use one primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. She had picked the settler's diary because it was the shortest item on the list, and now she had forty minutes before the bus left.

The diary belonged to a woman named Esther Rowe, who had written it in 1863 while traveling to Nebraska. Lucy leaned close to read the yellowed page through the glass. "We sold the shop in Ohio," Esther had written. "Papa says the land call is our last chance, and Mama cried but packed the wagon anyway." Lucy copied the words into her notebook. Land call. She had never heard that phrase before.

She found Mr. Delgado at the front desk, but he was already busy explaining the map room to another class, and she didn't want to intervene while he was mid-sentence. Instead she went to the wall of reproduced documents near the exit. A printed poster hung there, an old government notice. She read it twice. The Homestead Act of 1862, it said, offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on it and farmed it for five years. Lucy wrote down every word of that too.

Back at the case, she tested the idea against Esther's diary. If the law gave away land, then "land call" might mean that offer. She checked the later pages. In an entry dated the following spring, Esther had written, "Papa filed our claim at the land office. One hundred sixty acres, and if we stay five years and break the sod, it is ours." Lucy felt the two sources click together like puzzle pieces. The diary showed the want; the poster showed the reason behind it.

A boy from her class, Marcus, wandered over and looked at the case. "What's that thing?"

"A primary source," Lucy said. "Esther Rowe's diary. She moved west because of this law."

"That's it? A law made her move?"

"Not made her. Offered her land." Lucy pointed at her notebook. "Her dad owned a shop that was doing badly, and the law gave them a farm if they stayed on it. That's the whole answer, I think."

Marcus read her notes and nodded slowly. "Huh. So the diary is like the inside of it, and the poster is the outside."

"That's a simile," Lucy said, "and it's actually a good one."

On the way to the bus, Lucy kept thinking about Esther's last entry, written from a sod house with walls of dirt. "The wind makes the house feel vulnerable," Esther had written, "but Papa says nothing worth having comes easy." Lucy sat by the window and underlined that line twice. Then she opened her notebook to a fresh page and titled it: Why They Went.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
story:
Rachel set the steel ball at the top of the ramp and checked the meter stick one more time. The science fair was in four days, and her project depended on one number: how fast the ball rolled across the lab table after it left the ramp. She had marked a start line and a finish line exactly two meters apart, and her friend Dev stood ready with a stopwatch.

"Go," she said, and let the ball roll.

Dev clicked the stopwatch and read it out. "2.1 seconds." Rachel wrote it down and worked the division on her calculator. Two meters in 2.1 seconds was about 0.95 meters per second. She plotted the point on her distance-time graph, drew the line up from zero, and taped the sheet to the cabinet door. It looked good. One more run and she could call the data collection done.

The second run, the ball clipped a pencil someone had left near the finish line. "4.8 seconds," Dev said, frowning at the watch. Rachel stared at the number. At that time, the ball's speed came out to barely 0.42 meters per second, less than half the first result. If she drew that second point on her graph, her line would bend like a broken branch. Her whole display would look wrong, and the judges would ask why.

She almost crossed it out and kept only the first run. Then she stopped. One clean run and one mess of a run told her nothing about which one was real. She cleared the pencil off the table, and they ran the ball five more times. The readings came out 2.0, 2.2, 2.1, 2.0, and 2.1 seconds. Only the 4.8 stood apart, alone and wrong.

"So what do we write down?" Dev asked.

"We average the good ones," Rachel said. "Averaging repeated measurements gives a more reliable result than a single try." She added the six readings, minus the 4.8, divided by six, and got about 2.08 seconds. That made her speed 0.96 meters per second, almost exactly her first run. She drew a straight line on the graph through zero and up to two meters at 2.08 seconds, and the line sat clean and flat-sloped on the page.

At the fair, a judge in glasses leaned over her poster, where the graph hung beside the ramp. "Your table shows seven readings but only six in your average," she said. "Why is that one circled?"

"That one hit a pencil," Rachel said. "The rest I repeated and averaged."

The judge tapped the straight line on the graph and moved on to the next poster.

story:
Mr. Ruiz dropped a photocopy of a diary page on each desk and said the essay was due Friday: use the diary to explain why people moved west. Justin stared at the spidery handwriting and felt his stomach drop. He was good at math, not at reading some dead settler's chicken scratch.

The diary belonged to a woman named Hannah Voss, who had left Ohio in 1865 with her husband and three children. Justin squinted at the faded ink during study hall. "The ox's front leg went lame," he read slowly. "Samuel cut the swollen tendon and packed it with mud, but I fear we must put the poor creature down. Without him we cannot pull the wagon, and the seed corn we carry will not germinate in this heat."

His friend Priya leaned over. "You look like you're reading a foreign language."

"I am. Sort of." He tapped the page. "Look, she's crying about an ox. Why does that matter?"

"Because if the ox dies, they're stuck," Priya said. "Duh."

"But that's the answer, isn't it? Everything on the trail could kill the trip. An ox, a river, a fever." Justin sat up. The question was why people moved, but maybe the better question was why they stopped moving, or didn't. The diary showed the wagon road as a gauntlet.

At the school library he found a book about railroads, and one line stopped him cold: the first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed on 10 May 1869 at Promontory Summit, Utah, making the trip west far faster than by wagon. He counted on his fingers. Hannah Voss had taken seven months to get from Ohio to Wyoming, burying one child on the way. After that date in May 1869, somebody could ride the train west in days instead of months.

"So the diary explains half of it," he told Priya on Thursday, waving his rough draft. "People wanted land. But the diary also shows the cost, and the train changed the cost. Same want, easier road."

"That's actually not terrible," Priya admitted.

"Careful, that's practically a compliment."

He got an A minus on Monday, the best grade he'd earned all semester in history. Mr. Ruiz read a paragraph aloud to the class, about Hannah Voss and the lame ox and the trains that came later. Justin's ears burned; he stared at his desk and grinned at the wood grain. At lunch he pulled out the diary photocopy to show his little sister, then remembered she'd already gone on the bus. He folded the page into his pocket instead, next to his bus pass, and headed for the doors.

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
story:
Dominic stood at the foul line of the school gym with a stack of note cards in one hand and a basketball under his arm, because Coach Reyes had said the debate team could use the gym until five, and five was still twenty minutes away. His partner, Priya, sat on the bleachers sorting their cards into piles. Their case argued that the school should replace the diesel buses with electric ones, and their first card read: "Claim: Electric buses are better for the local ecosystem." The second card was a quote from a study about tailpipe emissions. The third card was blank.

"You're supposed to have a warrant for each point," Priya called down. "The claim, the evidence, and then the reason the evidence proves the claim. That's the whole structure."

"I know the structure," Dominic said. He bounced the basketball once and caught it. What he did not know was what to write on the blank cards. Last week he had watched a practice round in the library, and he remembered the team arguing for a new rule about phone lockers. Their speaker had finished, folded her arms, and said, "Unless the other side can prove this is a bad idea, we win." The opposing team had looked at each other, and the judge had leaned forward and said one word: "Burden." Nobody in the room had explained it, and the proposing team had lost that round.

Dominic set the basketball on the floor and walked the length of the gym, thinking. His side wanted the change. They wanted new buses. That meant the other side did not have to prove the old buses were fine. He had to prove the change was needed, all by himself, before anyone else said a word. He stopped at the far wall.

"Priya," he said. "Flip it around. Their coach is going to stand up there and say nothing, and if our case is empty, they win without talking."

"That's not possible," Priya said, but she was already frowning at her piles.

"It is. We're the ones proposing the change, so we carry the burden of proof. We have to show why it's needed instead of them proving it isn't." He jogged back to the bleachers, picked up the blank card, and wrote: "Warrant: because the study shows the diesel buses transport six hundred students past the wetland every day, the emissions enter that ecosystem, so switching buses directly reduces the harm." The words crowded the card and his handwriting slanted downhill, but the logic held together when he read it aloud.

"Say the whole point," Priya said.

"Electric buses are better for the local ecosystem. The evidence shows diesel emissions settle into the wetland the buses drive past. That means the evidence proves the claim, because the buses transport students past it twice a day, every day."

Priya wrote a warrant on her card too, then read his over his shoulder. "It works," she said. "It's stubborn, the way you made the connection do all the work, but it works."

"Obstinate," Dominic said. "It has to be. If I leave one hole, they'll stand up there, say nothing, and take the round."

The custodian pushed the door open at the far end of the gym and pointed at the clock. Dominic picked up the basketball, tucked the cards into his back pocket, and said, "Same time tomorrow. I want three more warrants before Friday."

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
story:
Arthur slid the photocopy across the library table and pressed it flat with both palms, as if the paper might bolt. "We have twenty minutes before we present," he said. "Ms. Ruiz wants each of us to paraphrase a speech into modern English, and I still can't figure out one word."

Priya leaned over from the next chair. "Which word?"

"Look." Arthur tapped the page. "It says 'I love thee' in one line, then 'thou art' in the next, then 'thee' again, then 'thou.' Shakespeare keeps switching. Is it random? Is it poetry stuff? If I read this out loud and get it wrong in front of everyone, I'll sound like an idiot."

Priya squinted at the lines. Marcus, sprawled at the end of the table with his hood up, pulled it down. "Maybe he just liked variety. Like using three different names for the same snack."

Arthur didn't think so. Shakespeare was careful about everything else, all the rhythm and the rhymes. He flipped to the back of the scene where the modern-translation help sheet sat, but the sheet only gave meanings, not reasons. He read the speech again, mouthing it, and noticed something. Every time the line said "I do something to somebody," the somebody was "thee." "I love thee. I trust thee. I give thee my heart." But when the somebody was doing something, it was "thou." "Thou art fair. Thou hast my heart." The pattern held for six lines straight.

He grabbed a pencil and wrote beneath the speech: "I love thee = I love you." Then, to test it, he wrote "You love me." Not "you love I." His pencil stopped. He said it out loud, half to himself. "Thee is the object form of thou, the way me is the object form of I."

Marcus sat up straight. "Say that again?"

"Thee is the object form of thou, the way me is the object form of I. That's why it changes. It's not variety. It's grammar." Arthur felt his ears go warm. "Thou does the action, thee gets the action done to it. Just like I and me."

"Okay, so how do we use that?" Priya checked the clock above the biography shelves. "Fifteen minutes."

"Instead of translating word by word, we condense each line into what it means now. 'I love thee' is 'I love you.' 'Thou art fair' is 'you're beautiful.' If we know which one does the action, we can't get it backwards." Arthur wrote fast, filling the margin, crossing out clumsy first tries and tightening them until each paraphrase sounded like something a person would actually say. Marcus suggested "you've got my heart," and Priya argued that "you have stolen my heart" was more authentic to the tone, so they kept hers.

At the front of the room, Priya held the original so Arthur could see it. He read the old lines first, then the new ones, and when he said "I love you, and I trust you, and you hold my heart," nobody laughed. A girl in the second row nodded slowly, and Ms. Ruiz wrote something on her clipboard.

"Where did you learn that thou and thee rule?" she asked afterward.

"Nowhere," Arthur said. "It was already in the speech. I just watched what the words were doing."

Marcus clapped him on the shoulder as they packed up. "Same time next month?"

"Book club meets on the second Thursday," Priya said, zipping her bag. "Don't make me paraphrase you into someone who shows up."

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
story:
Nathan stood in the kitchen with his science notes spread across the table and a problem the size of the monsoon itself. His presentation was due Friday, and he still could not picture how a wind could change direction just because the land got hot. He understood the words on the page, but the page was not the point. "You have to explain it," his mom kept saying, "like the class has never heard of it."

His older brother Ben sat at the counter with his eyes closed. Ben had taken a concussion at soccer practice two weeks earlier, and the doctor had said no screens, no reading, no bright lights, which meant Ben was bored enough to listen to anything. "Go ahead," Ben said. "I'm your practice audience. But you have to make me see it, because I can't look at your poster."

Nathan retrieved a baking pan from the garage and a bag of dry dirt from the potting shelf, plus a second pan of plain water. He set both on the sunny back steps and laid the thermometer from the medicine cabinet across each one in turn. While they sat, he showed Ben the photographs he had printed, wide green fields gleaming like shallow lakes. "That's rice," Nathan said. "Those flooded fields are called paddies." Ben squinted at the picture. "Why would anyone drown their crop on purpose?" Nathan checked his notes again. "The standing water keeps a lot of the weeds from growing," he said, and for the first time the fact felt like something he owned instead of something he was borrowing.

Every few minutes he ran out and read the thermometer. The dry dirt climbed fast in the sun, but the pan of water warmed slowly and kept its cool longer after the steps went into shadow. He wrote the numbers down, and the hidden thing he could not see finally made sense to him. Land heats up quickly, ocean water slowly, and the difference pulls moist air from the sea toward the hot land, carrying the rain. It was not magic and it was not a switch somebody flipped. It was a pattern, and he had caught a piece of it with two pans on a step.

"That part works," Ben admitted. "But is it a legitimate explanation if your pans are tiny and the Bay of Bengal is enormous?" Nathan said that was exactly what he would tell the class, that his pans were a small model of something too big to bring indoors. Ben smiled without opening his eyes. "That'll do."

At dinner Nathan was still rehearsing under his breath when his mom came in from the backyard with her shoes squelching. The garden hose, the one he had used to fill his pans and then left running, had soaked half the lawn and was creeping toward the tomato bed. She stood in the doorway, dripping, and looked straight at him. "Congratulations, Nathan," she said. "You've made it rain before you've even explained it."

story:
Alex had until Monday to figure out why his family, the Hendersons, would leave Ohio in 1843 for a trail that had already killed two of their neighbors, and his poster board was still blank. He sat on the cool granite steps of the war memorial with the photocopied diary pages spread across his knees, because the library had closed at four and his house was too loud. The diary belonged to a settler named Ruth Henderson, and so far Alex had read three pages about wagon axles.

The memorial was quiet except for water trickling into the stone basin behind him, and the smell of cut grass drifted over from the courthouse lawn. A woman in a volunteer's polo shirt was straightening the wreaths by the wall of names. When the wind flipped Alex's pages, she hurried over and set a smooth river rock on top of them. "The breeze gets sly around this corner," she said. "My husband was the same way about his genealogy papers. I've got a clipboard in the box if you want it."

Alex thanked her and clipped the pages down. He read on, hunting for the assignment's magic words, reasons, and finding nothing but mud and a broken wheel. Then, halfway down the fourth page, he stopped. Ruth had written, "Papa says the bank has taken the farm, and there is nothing here for us now. The Panic of 1837 ruined him, and everyone says the land out west is cheap and the soil is black and deep as a grave is long. Mama cried all night, but this morning she was packing."

Alex read the line again. He had expected something dramatic, a hunger for adventure, maybe. Instead there was a bank taking a farm, and a word he didn't know. Panic of 1837. He looked it up on his mom's old phone, holding it in the shade to see the screen, and found that the Panic of 1837 had caused a long economic depression across the whole United States. He sat with that for a minute, watching the water circle the basin. It was like a recession, the article said, except it lasted for years, and it wrecked farmers first. That was it. That was the whole answer hiding under the broken-wheel pages. They hadn't wanted the dangerous trail. They had lost everything back east, and the cheap, fertile land out west was the only door left open.

He wrote at the top of his poster, in careful block letters, WHY THEY LEFT, and underneath, Ruth's line about the bank, word for word, the way his teacher said primary sources should be quoted. The volunteer came back with a thermos and poured him a cup of cocoa, because the wind had turned cold. "You look like a boy who just found something," she said.

"I think I found the fundamental reason," Alex said, tapping the diary. "They didn't move west because they wanted to. They had to resign themselves to the trail after the Panic of 1837 ruined them. That's the whole story." He slid the diary copy across the stone so she could read it too.

story:
Brooke had ten dollars of birthday money and a presentation due Monday on the difference between simple and compound interest, and she was spending both at the mall. Her best friend Priya worked Saturdays at the smoothie kiosk near the food court, and Brooke figured she could practice her slides on someone while she decided what to buy.

"Here's my opener," Brooke said, leaning on the counter between a mango order and a guy waiting for wheatgrass. "Albert Einstein called compound interest the eighth wonder of the world."

"Did he?" Priya said. She accommodated a customer who wanted extra honey, then came back wiping her hands on her apron. "Did you check? My brother lost a whole grade on a history paper last year because he used a quote nobody actually said."

Brooke pulled out her phone. At the table by the escalator, with a strawberry-banana smoothie melting beside her, she searched the quote. The first three websites repeated it proudly, all with Einstein's name in bold. The fourth was different. It said the saying was often credited to Einstein, but there was no reliable evidence he ever said it. She read the sentence twice, then found the same claim on two more credible sources. Not one of them could point to a time, a place, or a document where he'd said it.

"Great," she muttered. Her whole presentation was built on that opener. But then she sat with it, turning the smoothie cup in her hands. Actually, she thought, this was better. She could tell the class the quote was probably fake, and then show them the numbers, which didn't need a famous name to be impressive. Simple interest meant the bank paid you five percent of your original deposit every year, the same flat amount, forever. Compound interest meant the bank paid five percent on everything in the account, including the interest already added. She sketched it out on a napkin: deposit one hundred dollars, and after five years the simple account grew in a straight, stubborn line, while the compound one curved upward, bending away like the escalator railing rising over her head. The one variable that mattered most was time. The longer the money sat, the wider the gap.

She tried a small test to make sure she understood it herself. With simple interest, one hundred dollars at five percent earned five dollars a year, so twenty-five dollars over five years, no more. With compounding, the first year also earned five dollars, but the second year earned five twenty-five, because the interest itself earned interest, and by year five the total was more than a hundred and twenty-seven. She checked the math twice, both on the napkin and in a calculator app, because if she was going to tell a class that Einstein probably never said the thing everyone quoted, her own numbers had better be right.

She spent the ten dollars on a binder for her printed slides, walked back to the kiosk, and slid the napkin across the counter to Priya. "New opener," she said. "Want to hear the one Einstein never said?"

activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
story:
Haraper had done everything wrong in the right order, which was almost worse than doing it wrong at all. Her portrait of Mr. Bexley, the art room's ancient stuffed parrot, had started well: a pale wash of yellow for the base, then a deeper layer for shadow, exactly the way the handout said, light to dark. But somewhere around the third wash she had put a fat blue blob right on the beak, and now she was staring at it while Milo leaned over her shoulder making sympathetic horse noises.

"Just paint a bigger parrot around it," he suggested.

"That's vain," said a voice from the sink, where Priya was washing brushes, "thinking a mistake is too beautiful to lose."

"That is not what vain means," said Harper, without turning around. "And it's the beak, Milo. The beak is the whole parrot."

She dipped her smallest brush in clean water and touched it to the blob's edge to soften it. To her horror, the dried blue smeared, blooming outward like a bruise. "Wait. That paint was dry. I watched it dry. Why is it moving?" She touched it again, and more blue came off onto her brush tip.

Priya wandered over, dripping. "My grandma paints. She says watercolour isn't like other paint. It's pigment bound with gum arabic, and that lets it dissolve again in water even after it has dried."

Harper looked at her ruined beak. Then she looked at her brush, which was now tipped with blue. Then she did the math out loud. "So if water turns dried paint back into paint, I don't need a bigger parrot. I need a wet one." She brushed clean water carefully over the blob, counted to five, and blotted it with a paper towel. The blue lifted, most of it, leaving only a ghost of a smudge.

"You're a genius," said Milo.

"I'm a scientist," said Harper, and went back in with water, lifting and blotting until the ghost faded too. "And now I emphasize the beak with a nice opaque gray, painted last, because last layers are the boss layers." She laid down a fresh dark edge along the top of the beak where it met the feathers, and Mr. Bexley, stuffed and one-eyed and faintly ridiculous, finally looked like he might bite someone.

At the end of class she hung the portrait on the drying rack between Milo's lopsided clay elephant and Priya's painting of what Milo insisted was a potato but Priya swore was her brother. "You know," Milo said, squinting at the parrot, "from far away that could almost be real cartilage in the beak."

"It's paper, Milo."

"From far away," he said again, and backed slowly out of the room.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
story:
Grandpa's binoculars were already aimed at the fence post when Colton jogged out onto the porch. "Hawk's back," Grandpa whispered, like it was breaking news. "Sharp-shinned. Predatory little thing, but efficient. Watch him work that field." Colton grabbed the second pair of binoculars and found the hawk, gray and quick, riding the wind without flapping once. Any other Saturday he would have been glued to that bird for an hour. Today his mind kept sliding back to the lunchroom at school.

Yesterday, Derek had done his imitation of Marcus's stutter, dragging out the ssssound until half the table laughed, and Colton had laughed too, just a little, because it was easier than arguing. Then in last period Ms. Reyes had put two words on the board, upstander and bystander, and asked which one people had been that day. Colton had stared at his desk so hard he nearly wore a hole in it.

"Grandpa," he said, still watching the hawk, "if you watch somebody get picked on and don't do anything, what's that called?" Grandpa lowered his binoculars. "Bystander. An upstander's the opposite, someone who speaks up or acts to support the person being mistreated instead of only watching." He squinted at Colton. "Why?"

Colton told him, all of it, even the part where he laughed. His face went hot, but Grandpa just nodded. "You know we're descendants of a woman who ran a stop on the Underground Railroad through this county? Sat right there in that cellar with people she didn't know, spoke up with her whole house." He tapped the porch floor twice. "Course, she had practice. Started small, I'd bet."

That night Colton tested an idea. If speaking up felt impossible in front of a whole table, maybe it worked like the hawk: pick the exact moment, move fast, don't hover. He texted Marcus, "Hey, Derek's imitation yesterday was garbage. Sorry I laughed. Want to sit with me Monday?" The reply came back in under a minute: "yeah actually. thanks."

Monday, in the lunch line, Derek started up again, honking out his fake stutter. Colton's stomach dropped, but he stepped over anyway. "Derek. Knock it off, man, it's old." Then, before Derek could spin it into a joke about him, Colton turned to Marcus. "Dude, did you finish that level in Starforge? You said it was impossible." Marcus grinned and started talking, and Derek, with no show left to perform for, wandered off.

On the way to the trash cans, their friend Priya caught up. "That was actually cool. Bystanders just stand there, but you were an upstander." Marcus balanced his tray on one hand. "And I got a lunch buddy out of it, so everybody wins," he said. "Except Derek."

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
story:
Riley set her pencil down, stared at her outline sheet, and read her three points aloud in a whisper. "One: the school should add a second water fountain near the gym. Two: one fountain makes long lines. Three: students wait too long for water after practice." She frowned. Something about that felt wrong, like a sock seam twisted inside her shoe.

The library smelled like old glue and floor wax, and the late afternoon light came in parallel stripes across the table where she sat. Her friend Marcus dropped into the chair across from her with his own paper, because Ms. Okafor had paired them as peer reviewers before anyone got to draft.

"Read me yours," Marcus said. "But just the outline. She said the thesis and the points, no draft."

Riley read the three points again, slowly this time, and watched his face. When she finished, Marcus tapped the page. "Wait. Two and three are the same thing."

"No, they're not. One's about lines, one's about waiting."

"Lines are waiting," Marcus said. "You just said it two different ways."

Riley opened her mouth to argue, then closed it. She read the points once more, this time asking herself a quiet question: if I deleted point two, would point three still be true? It would. That was the problem. "So my argument isn't really three points at all," she said. "It's two. The second one is just wearing a disguise."

Marcus shrugged. "So find a real third one. Like, fountains are cheap? Or thirsty athletes play worse?"

Riley exhaled and pulled out a fresh sheet. The cheap idea felt boring, and she couldn't find any proof that thirst made her teammates play worse, though she privately suspected it after last Tuesday's loss. She wrote and crossed out, wrote and crossed out. What else did she actually know? She thought about the custodian, Mr. Alvarez, hauling his cart down the far hallway every single afternoon because the gym hallway had no water source at all. That was different. Lines were about time, but this was about place. She wrote: three, the far side of the building has no water source, so students cross the whole school to drink.

"Read it now," Marcus said. She did, and he nodded. "Yeah. If you deleted any one of those, the others would still stand. They're really different reasons."

Riley grinned and started her draft, the thesis sentence sitting at the top of the page like a key that finally fit its lock. Then Marcus slid his own outline across the table for her to check, and she read his three points about why the school should keep its late bus. One: it helps athletes. Two: it lets kids without rides stay for clubs. Three: kids who play sports need a way home.

She looked up at him. "Marcus. Your two and your three."

He snatched the paper back and stared at it. "Oh no."

"Oh yes," Riley said, and slid her eraser across the table to him.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
story:
Jack spread his homework sheet across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with the salt shaker and a mug. The assignment said to pick one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and explain it in his own words, which sounded easy until he actually opened the booklet his teacher had printed. The pages were dense, and the print was so small he had to squint.

"You look like you're defusing a bomb," his mother said, setting a bowl of cereal beside him.

"It's the Charter. I have to explain a right in my own words, but the rights all sound the same when I read them." He flipped pages with meticulous care, because the booklet belonged to the school and the corners were already soft. "There are so many of them. How am I supposed to pick?"

"Pick one that matters to you," she said. She was lacing her shoes by the door, wallet in hand, because today was one of the advance voting days and she wanted to beat the after-work crowd.

That gave Jack an idea. His mother was going to vote right now, at this very minute, so voting had to be a right somewhere in these pages. He ran his finger down the sections until he found it. Section 3. Every citizen of Canada has the right to vote in elections for members of the House of Commons or of a legislature. He read it twice, then copied the number onto his page so he wouldn't lose it.

"Wait," he called. "When you get there, can you text me a picture of the sign at the door? The one about who's allowed to vote?"

His mother raised an eyebrow. "Homework or spy mission?"

"Test," Jack said. "I want to see if the sign matches what the Charter says."

She laughed and left, and Jack kept reading while he waited. His grandmother's letter had come that morning, and it sat propped against the fruit bowl, so he read it a second time while he ate. Her handwriting described her own street on election day, the seniors' van shuttle from her building and the poll worker who carried a folding chair out to the sidewalk for Mr. Petrucci, who could not stand in line long. There is a ramp now where the steps used to be, she wrote. Little things, Jackie, but they signify that somebody thought about people like us.

His phone buzzed. His mother had sent a photo: a laminated sign taped beside the polling station entrance. It said voters must be Canadian citizens, and it listed the elections people were voting in that day, the House of Commons and the provincial legislature. Jack held the booklet up beside the screen and compared, line by line. Section 3 said every citizen could vote in elections for the House of Commons or a legislature. The sign said the same thing in plainer words. His test had worked, and the match told him his explanation was on the right track.

He wrote his paragraph fast, before the feeling could leak away: In Canada, being a citizen means you get to help choose the people who make the laws, both for the whole country and for your province. He read it aloud once. Then he typed back to his mother, "It matches. Thanks. Bring me something from the bakery?" and set the phone down next to his grandmother's letter, which he decided he would answer tonight.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
story:
On Saturday mornings the women's side of the mosque was quiet enough to hear the fans turn, and Laurence sat on the carpet with her surah sheet spread flat, whispering the same six verses for the third week running. She had to recite them without the paper at her coming-of-age ceremony in June, and every time she got to the fourth verse, the words slid out of order like beads off a snapped thread.

Her cousin Rania, who was nineteen and home from her second year of college, dropped onto the carpet beside her with a bottle of water. "Still stuck on the same page?"

"Same verse," Laurence said. "It's like it erases itself overnight."

"Try me," Rania said. "I'll recite with you." She closed her eyes and began, and the words came out smooth and certain, verse after verse, far past the six on the sheet, on into chapters Laurence had never even opened. Laurence stopped mouthing along and just listened.

"You know all of it?" she asked when Rania finished.

"All 114 chapters, every one," Rania said. "It took four years. Once you've done it, you're called a hafiz."

"Then it's done forever," Laurence said. "You could forget about it and just recite at the ceremony like breathing."

Rania laughed and shook her head, but she didn't explain, and that annoyed Laurence, so she decided to test it herself. For two weeks she made a private list of which verses she asked for and when. She asked Rania for the same difficult passage on a Friday after her long chemistry lab, and Rania hesitated, restarted once, and got a phrase in the wrong place. On Sunday, after a whole quiet morning at home, Laurence asked again, and the same passage came out flawless. She flipped back through her notes. Every shaky recitation lined up with a busy day or a missed morning; every clean one followed a day Rania had practiced, even for half an hour. There was the pattern, invisible until she'd written it down. Memorizing wasn't a box you filled once. It was more like her mother's income from the market stall, which vanished unless new money kept coming in.

The week of the ceremony, an aunt tried to rearrange the program so a boy from the family would recite the opening instead of Laurence, saying the audience trusted a male voice better. Rania stepped in before anyone could answer her. "You're being biased," she said. "Laurence has prepared the recitation, so Laurence gives it." The aunt threw up her hands and sat down.

Laurence stood at the front with no paper in her hands, took a breath, and began at verse one, the words arriving in their right order, every one.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
story:
Oliver had promised his grandfather he would finish the science project before the harvest festival, and now the festival was two days away and the project was a mess. He sat at the workbench in the barn with the old brass microscope his grandfather kept in a wooden case, and beside him lay a letter his science teacher had sent home: "Oliver has the focus to do this well. He needs to slow down." He read it twice and folded it small.

The onion came from the crate by the door. He peeled off the thin inner skin, the piece that is almost transparent, and laid a square of it on the slide with a drop of water. Then he lowered the coverslip flat, all at once, and pressed his eye to the lens. The field was crowded with round shapes, each one ringed in black. He grabbed his notebook and started to draw them, labeling the first one "cell," then hesitated. Last month he had labeled a dust speck as a paramecium, and his grandfather had laughed for a whole evening. He was not going to guess twice.

He called through the barn door to Marisol, who was helping her uncle at the farm stand across the lane. She came over wiping her hands on her jeans and took a look. "Those aren't cells," she said. "Those are air bubbles. My cousin did the same thing last year." Oliver sat back. Round, dark-edged circles, and every one of them empty inside. He thought about how the coverslip had dropped flat, trapping whatever was underneath it.

He lifted the coverslip, added a fresh drop of water, and tried again, this time lowering one edge first so the glass tilted down over the onion skin at an angle, edge by edge. When he looked through the lens, the bubbles were nearly gone. The cells lay in rows like bricks, each one a neat rectangle. He drew them, then hunted along the outer edge of one cell until he found the wall, the thin membrane just inside it, and a dark dot deep in the middle that had to be the nucleus. "The nucleus," Marisol said, pointing. "That's what my cousin called the dot." He labeled all three, and his handwriting was careful, nothing arbitrary about it, because a diagram with a wrong label is worse than a blank one.

"You know he only teases you because he thinks you can take it," Marisol said, watching him fill in the last label. She was talking about his grandfather, and they both knew it, but Oliver kept his eyes on the page. His grandfather had wanted him to be an artisan at this the way he was with wood, patient and exact, and Oliver had mostly wanted to be finished. He thought of the letter folded in his pocket, the words "slow down," and how tonight he would stand at the kitchen table and decide whether to hand it over before or after he showed the slide.

He carried the microscope out into the evening light, Marisol walking beside him with the onion skin still thin and curled in the jar. "Draw it one more time," she said. "From the side, so you can see the angle." Oliver took out his pencil.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
story:
Rosalie stood in the wings of the school auditorium with forty minutes until the improv demonstration for the seventh graders, and her partner, Marcus, was reading the rules off a crumpled handout. "Accept every offer," he said. "You have to say yes, and. So if I say we're in a submarine, you say yes, and the sonar is beeping." Rosalie nodded, though she privately thought the rule sounded too simple to be the whole game.

Their first practice scene collapsed in seconds. Marcus opened a refrigerator, so Rosalie opened a mailbox, and they stood in two different worlds until the scene just stopped, like a watch with a broken spring. "We have to agree on where we are," she said. "That's the yes part. But there's something else." She watched the older kids from drama club warming up on stage, the way one girl would say "Doctor, my arm hurts" and suddenly the other kid checked the elbow, pressed a tendon near the wrist, and acted like a physician. The words themselves seemed to hand over a role, like passing a baton.

She tested it. In the next scene Marcus froze, blank as a dropped curtain, so Rosalie turned to him and said, "Captain, the engines are failing." His posture changed before his face did. He gripped an invisible wheel, barked orders, and steered them through a meteor shower. When they finished he blinked. "You made me the captain. How?"

"It's called endowing," said Priya from the front row, without looking up from her phone. "You give your partner a role through what you say."

Rosalie turned it over while Priya called five minutes. Every time a scene had worked this afternoon, somebody had endowed first. The doctor, the captain, one kid who got called "the world's most competent window washer" and immediately began spraying an imaginary squeegee. The pattern corresponded so neatly to success that she wondered why nobody had mentioned it sooner, then remembered that the handout was crumpled in Marcus's pocket and probably had three more rules they'd never read.

At the demonstration, the two of them walked out under the hot lights. Marcus leaned toward her. "You start," he whispered, which was dangerous, because if she opened a scene wrong they'd both freeze in front of two hundred seventh graders. Rosalie thought of the doctor, the captain, the window washer. She took a breath and pointed at the empty space beside her.

"Museum guard," she said, "the dinosaur skeleton is walking out the front door."

Marcus squared his shoulders. "Then we'd better catch it before it reaches the parking lot."

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
story:
Grayson slid his French textbook across the library table and glared at it like it had insulted his family. On Friday, his class was going to a French café where everyone had to order lunch in French, ask the price, and get the bill, all without switching to English. His friend Priya had already promised to film anyone who froze mid-sentence, so the stakes could not have been higher.

"Ordering food is easy," Priya said, dropping into the chair across from him with her own book. "The hard part is the bill. What do you even say?"

Grayson flipped to the back of the book, where the vocabulary lists lived. "La facture," he read. "That's invoice. Or la note. That's like a note." He wrote both on a scrap of paper, feeling pleased with himself. How hard could it be? You pointed at cake, you said the price, you asked for the note. It felt almost too easy, which should have been his first warning.

Priya leaned over and squinted at his paper. "La note? That sounds like something you pass to someone in class." She grinned. "Are you going to ask the waiter for a secret message?"

"That's a naive thing to say about French," Grayson said, jabbing his pencil at her. "Words have more than one meaning. Fine is an English word and also a penalty. It's a pattern." But even as he said it, a small doubt wiggled in the back of his mind. French restaurants were probably not full of people asking for invoices. There had to be a restaurant word, something he was missing, and it was hiding somewhere outside the vocabulary chapter.

He marched to the computer catalog, typed in "French phrasebook," and found a skinny orange book shelved in travel. He carried it back, sat down, and ran his finger down the restaurant section. There it was, printed in bold: L'addition, s'il vous plaît. Underneath, in smaller type: The bill, please. Not la facture. Not la note. Addition. He said it out loud three times, quietly, because the librarian had already given him one warning look.

"Find it?" Priya asked.

"If you'd asked for la facture," Grayson said, "the waiter would probably think you wanted paperwork." He copied the phrase onto a menu he'd drawn himself: a croissant, a sandwich, and one suspiciously large slice of cake. Then he paraphrased the whole exchange into the simplest possible version so Priya could practice too. "You say je voudrais, then the food, then combien ça coûte, then l'addition, s'il vous plaît. That's the whole show."

Priya picked up the paper menu and gave his drawing a serious critique. "The croissant looks like a deflated seashell. Otherwise, perfect."

Grayson snatched it back, cleared his throat, and delivered his order to the pencil sharpener as if it were a Parisian waiter. "Je voudrais le gâteau. L'addition, s'il vous plaît!"

From three tables away, the librarian called out, "En français, s'il vous plaît," without looking up, and Priya laughed so hard she slid halfway under the table.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
story:
Katherine sat cross-legged on Priya's bedroom floor with Priya's laptop balanced on a stack of board games, staring at a column of numbers. They had spent the whole week selling lemonade at the end of Priya's driveway, and Priya had typed each day's earnings into the spreadsheet: Monday in B2, Tuesday in B3, all the way to Sunday in B10. Katherine wanted a chart to show their class which day earned the most, but first she had to add the column, and she was not going to punch seven numbers into a calculator like a little kid.

"Try the equals sign," Priya said, chewing the end of her pencil. "My cousin does something with an equals sign."

Katherine typed =SUM(B2:B10) into an empty cell, copying it from a smudged index card her cousin had left at their lemonade stand. When she pressed Enter, the number 47.25 appeared. It looked right, but she wanted to verify it, so she added the seven numbers by hand on paper. Forty-seven dollars and twenty-five cents. The formula had done it in one step. She narrowed her eyes at the colon in the middle. "So B2 colon B10," she said slowly, "that must mean everything from B2 down to B10. All of it."

"That's why it worked and my way didn't," Priya said. Earlier she had typed =SUM(B2,B10), and the spreadsheet had answered 14.75, which was only Monday plus Sunday, as if the week had lasted just two days. The consequence of skipping the middle days would have been telling their class they earned barely anything. Katherine deleted Priya's version and kept her own, then clicked through the menus until a bar chart bloomed on the screen, seven bars, with Sunday towering over all the rest.

Then came the twist. Katherine pointed at the tall Sunday bar. "Why is Sunday so big?" Priya went quiet and pulled a folded twenty from her pocket. Her grandmother had bought six cups on her walk home from church, and Priya had written it down without saying anything. "I was going to split it with you," Priya said. "I just forgot to tell you." Katherine did the math in her head. Without Grandma, Sunday was the same as Saturday, and their whole total dropped to about twenty-seven dollars.

"So we made less than we thought," Katherine said, "but now we know the spreadsheet catches things." She updated the chart and printed two copies, one for each of them. The bars looked smaller than before, honest and a little disappointing, but the paper was still warm from the printer, and Priya handed over her half of the twenty without being asked. Katherine folded it into her pocket next to the index card. "Next week," she said, "we track expenses too."

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
story:
Easton spread his notes across the kitchen table like a general planning an invasion, which would have looked more impressive if half the notes were not covered in orange juice from the glass he had already knocked over once. His world religions teacher had assigned a compare-and-contrast project: pick two faiths and explain what each one says happens after death. Easton had picked Islam and Hinduism, mostly because his friend Dev claimed his grandmother knew everything about reincarnation and Easton's own neighbor, Mrs. Haddad, was coming over that afternoon to drop off a casserole dish. Research through casserole delivery struck him as efficient.

The problem was that the two ideas refused to line up. Dev had explained, mouth full of pretzels, that in Hinduism the soul comes back again and again, living many lives until it finally gets things right. Easton had written LIFE, THEN ANOTHER LIFE, THEN ANOTHER, PROBABLY TIRESOME on one index card. For Islam he had only a half sentence from his textbook, and the half sentence refused to cooperate. He flipped the card over, squinted at it, and ate a pretzel in a rebellious manner, as if the pretzel itself had opinions about theology.

When the doorbell rang, Easton answered it still holding his cards. Mrs. Haddad handed him the dish, spotted the cards, and read the half sentence upside down, which is a skill grandmothers and neighbors develop automatically. "Oh, you're stuck on the Judgment part," she said.

"Kind of. The book says something about a day and being raised, but it cuts off," Easton said. "Is it like a do-over day? Like, if you mess up one life, do you get another one?"

Mrs. Haddad laughed so hard she had to set the casserole on the counter to steady herself. "No do-overs, habibi. In Islam you get this one life. At the end there's a Day of Judgment. We call it Yawm al-Qiyamah." Easton scribbled it down, syllable by syllable, and underlined it twice, then a third time for luck.

That was the piece he'd been missing. One faith gave you many lives to improve; the other gave you a single life and then a verdict. He tested it right there at the counter with two glasses of water as stand-ins: the glass that kept getting refilled, and the glass that got poured once and then judged on whether he had drunk it politely or spilled it like an untrained golden retriever. Mrs. Haddad watched this demonstration with great seriousness. "The spilled glass goes to hell?" she asked.

"The spilled glass gets a stern talking-to," Easton said, mopping the counter. Dev was going to be so embarrassed that his pretzel-based lecture had left out the entire comparison. Easton could hardly wait to tell him.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
story:
Kayla stood at Grandma Rosa's counter with an onion in front of her and a knife in her hand, and she had one goal: make a pasta sauce good enough that her cousin Marco would stop bragging about the jar sauce from the store. Marco claimed nobody under seventy could cook from scratch. Kayla intended to prove him wrong by Saturday dinner.

"Curl your fingers under, like a claw," Grandma said, chopping air with her own hand to show her. "Knuckles guide the blade. Fingertips stay out of the way." Kayla curled her fingers and pressed her knuckles against the flat of the blade. The first cut wobbled and the half onion skidded toward the edge of the counter. The second cut landed clean, and the third after that. She could feel the rhythm of it, like a pattern hiding inside the onion, waiting for her hand to find it. She wondered if every skill had a hidden pattern like that, something you couldn't see until your fingers discovered it.

Then the worst thing happened. She reached for the salt shaker and her elbow knocked the knife. It slid off the counter, spinning, and every instinct in her screamed to grab it. Instead she jumped backward, and the knife hit the floor with a clang and lay there, gleaming and harmless. Her heart hammered. Grandma didn't even look up from her pot. "Good," she said. "If a knife starts to fall, you let it drop. Trying to catch a falling knife is how people get cut." Kayla picked it up, washed it, and set it flat in the center of the cutting board where it couldn't slide again. She noticed she had already revised her whole setup in her head, moving the salt to the other side too, so nothing else lived near the edge.

They crushed tomatoes with their hands, and Kayla watched the seeds pool at the bottom of the bowl like tiny amber beads. Grandma stirred, then held out the spoon. Kayla tasted. It was thin and pale and disappointing. "It tastes a little impoverished," she said. "Like it's missing something." Grandma laughed. "Salt, a pinch of sugar, and time. Flavor you can't rush." Kayla thought of Grandpa in the garden, who claimed onions were practically an antibiotic and would fix anything from a cold to a bad mood. She wasn't sure she believed him, but she sliced another onion anyway, claw grip and all, and stirred it into the pot.

By Saturday, Marco took one bite, paused, and took another. "This is from a jar," he said. Kayla set the knife down flat in the center of the counter and smiled. "Prove it."

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
story:
The folded note landed on Easton's shoe during the car ride, passed back from his best friend Marcus, whose church youth group was visiting the Hindu temple the same morning as Easton's social studies class. "Bet your grandma says people get reborn and that's the best part," Marcus had written. "Ask her if we'd WANT that." Easton grinned and wrote back, "Watch me."

Inside, the temple smelled of incense and flowers, and shoes sat in rows by the door like sleeping animals. Easton's grandmother, who taught the comparative religions unit at the community center and was considered something of a prestigious scholar in their neighborhood, had come along as a guide. Easton kept his notebook ready. He had decided to categorize everything he heard today: beliefs about heaven in one column, beliefs about rebirth in another, and a big question mark for everything else.

"That bell means the priest is waking the deity for the morning," his grandmother said, tilting her head toward the shrine. After the arati, when the flame circled and everyone sang, she answered questions from the group. A girl asked what happens when people die, and his grandmother said some here believe the soul is born again into a new life, and that this continues in a great cycle.

Marcus elbowed Easton hard. Easton raised his hand. "So being reborn, is that something you hope for, or something you want to get out of?"

"That's the question, isn't it?" his grandmother said, eyes sparkling like he'd won a prize. She turned to the priest's assistant, a young man arranging fruit near the altar. "Would you say it?"

The young man smiled. "Moksha is liberation from the cycle of rebirth," he said simply, "and it is the highest goal of human life."

Easton scribbled fast. No heaven column. He drew an arrow with LOOP crossed out next to it. Marcus leaned over and whispered, "So the best thing is to escape the loop? Our pastor says the best thing is going to be with God forever." Easton looked at his two columns, then at his question-mark column, and made a third heading: THE GOAL. Under rebirth he wrote "escape it"; under heaven he wrote "reach it." The arrow went the same direction on both, away from here, toward something higher. He practically bounced in his seat.

Back at the shoe rows, Marcus dug in his pocket. "Almost forgot. Second note." This one said, "My mom says ask your grandma if she'll do a swap, you come to our Easter service, I come back here." Easton looked up, and his grandmother was already reading over his shoulder.

"Tell his mother yes," she said. "And Marcus, you're a descendant of question-askers, all of you. That's the best lineage there is." She held the door, and the morning light hit the temple steps. "Next time, you two ask the questions together."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
story:
Adam slid into the seat beside the reference desk, where the library's only free computer waited, and pulled his crumpled worksheet from his backpack. The science club needed a chart of how much cafeteria waste each grade produced last month, and Mr. Ruiz had said whoever brought the best chart would get to present it at the assembly. Adam wanted that spot more than he wanted lunch, which was saying something.

He opened the spreadsheet and typed the numbers from his worksheet into column B, one row for each grade. Then he clicked the empty cell below the last number and typed SUM(B2:B10), exactly the way the handout showed. He pressed Enter. The cell did not show a total. It showed SUM(B2:B10), the letters sitting there like plain text, refusing to be anything else. Adam checked the handout three times. He had not mistyped anything.

He leaned toward the next computer, where a girl from his class, Priya, was typing fast. "Did your total work?" he asked.

She glanced over. "You forgot the equals sign. Every formula has to start with it. Without the equals sign, the cell just shows what you typed." She turned back to her screen, where a neat column of numbers already added itself.

Adam sat very still for a second, feeling both foolish and relieved. He deleted the cell, typed =SUM(B2:B10), and pressed Enter. The number 412 appeared instantly. He checked it against his worksheet, adding the rows by hand, and it matched. One small symbol had been the difference between words and a number. He was not going to forget it.

Then he highlighted the grades and their totals and clicked the chart button. A bar graph appeared, and the sixth-grade bar towered over the others because sixth graders threw out the most apple cores. Adam thought of the compost bin project, the one where worms and other decomposers turned food scraps into soil, and decided his chart should go right next to it. He saved the file, then went to retrieve his flash drive from the bottom of his backpack, digging past a smashed granola bar he had been negligent about cleaning out for weeks.

When he plugged in the drive and hit save again, the screen went gray. Priya looked over and laughed, not unkindly. "Autosave," she said. "Mine's been in the cloud the whole time."

Adam stared at the frozen screen, finger hovering over the power button, and whispered, "Please still be there."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
story:
The gymnasium smelled like vinegar and poster glue, which Jonathan took as a good sign, since his project involved both. His display read ACIDS, BASES, AND THE SECRET LIFE OF pH, and beside it sat twelve labeled cups: lemon juice, soap water, baking soda mixed with water, cola, milk, and seven more he had collected from his kitchen at midnight like an eccentric chemist raiding his own refrigerator. Each cup had a strip of litmus paper taped beside it, red where the paper had turned and blue where it hadn't. His plan was to let the judges evaluate his results themselves.

Marcus from fourth period strolled over with his own poster under his arm. He squinted at Jonathan's chart, where every cup had a number next to it. "What's the pH of that lemon juice?"

"Three," Jonathan said.

Marcus pointed at the cola cup, which read four. "So the cola's basically the same. Three and four, that's only a one apart." He smiled the way he did when he thought he'd caught something. "Your whole chart says lemon juice and cola are both just sour."

Jonathan looked at his chart, then at the two cups. Something in his stomach went tight, the way it did before a test he hadn't studied for. He had written the numbers down three days ago, but he had never really thought about what jumped between them. A one didn't look like much. He needed a way to show Marcus, right here, right now, with a judge already moving down the aisle toward them.

"Wait," Jonathan said. He pulled out his science notebook and flipped to the back page. "Every whole step on the pH scale is a tenfold change." He wrote 3, then 4, then drew an arrow between them and wrote x10 beside it. "So pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4. Not one more. Ten times."

Marcus frowned. "Ten times? From one number apart?"

"Ten times," Jonathan said. "That's the whole trick of the scale." He tore two fresh strips of litmus paper from his kit, because he wanted Marcus to see the numbers weren't just marks on a poster. He dipped one strip in the lemon juice and one in the cola and laid them side by side on the table. Both turned pink, but the lemon strip went deep red almost instantly, faster than the cola strip, and Jonathan felt his pulse slow down for the first time all morning. "It isn't a ladder where every step is the same size," he said. "It's more like each step is a whole flight of stairs."

Marcus leaned in so close his nose nearly touched the paper. "So my poster's wrong," he said quietly. "I wrote that pH 5 and pH 6 aquarium water are close enough."

The judge stopped at their table, clipboard ready, and tapped the lemon juice cup. "Walk me through your method."

Jonathan took a breath. "First I dip the litmus paper, then I read the color against the chart, then I record the pH number. Same steps every time, same order." He straightened the two pink strips next to each other, deep red beside pale rose, and slid them toward her. "See for yourself."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
story:
Brielle slid into the seat at the far computer in the lab and typed her program before the bell even finished ringing. It asked for a number, then tested every divisor from 2 up to the number itself, printing "prime" or "not prime." It worked on 7. It worked on 31. Then Marcus, her project colleague on this assignment, leaned over and typed 982,451,653.

The cursor blinked. And blinked. Brielle stared at the frozen screen. "It's stuck," she whispered.

"It's checking every single number up to nine hundred million," Marcus said. "We're going to be here until graduation."

Brielle grabbed her notebook. First fix: stop testing at the square root, since anything past that would have already found a partner. She added that, and the program sped up, but 982,451,653 still took a slow crawl. She squinted at her loop, counting on her fingers. Skip the even divisors, she thought. After checking 2, why test 4, 6, 8 at all? An odd number can never be divided evenly by an even one. So if the number isn't even, the program only needs odd divisors. She deleted half the checks and started the loop at 3, stepping by 2. She saved the file and held her breath.

The answer flashed back in under a second: not prime. "Look at that!" she said, loud enough that two kids at the next monitor turned around. "Twice as fast. We halved the work." Marcus magnified the timing numbers on his screen so the whole row could see the before-and-after, and he was already planning their next test. "Give me your phone number," he said. "If it's nine or ten digits, we can check it for prime factors before the bell."

Brielle started to laugh, then stopped. She typed her own number in, and the program thought for a moment and printed "prime." She tried her mother's number: prime. Then she typed the number from the gym locker she'd been assigned that morning, 316, and the program answered instantly, "not prime." She tried dividing it in her head by odd numbers after 2, the way the program did, and landed on 4 times 79. That meant her locker combination, which was supposed to be random, came from a number that factored neatly, and if it factored, someone with the same program could break it.

She looked at Marcus. "Tomorrow we test every locker number in the school."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
story:
The teasing started right after lunch, at the long table by the windows. Dex had knocked over his milk, and now Braden was drawing it out. "Nice job, spill king," Braden said, and two kids at the end of the table laughed. Dex stared at his tray and mopped at the puddle with one slow, lethargic swipe of his napkin.

Harper's first idea was to tell Braden to knock it off. She had tried that in October, when he was on Marcus about his shoes. Braden had just turned it around and started on her for a week. So she sat there and thought instead. Why did some teasing stop on its own and some keep going? She ran through the times she'd watched it. Once, when Braden was ragging on Priya's drawing, Ms. Okafor had walked past, and he'd quit instantly, but that was fear, not a fix. Then she remembered something odd from the fall party. Braden had been teasing Dex about his old backpack, and right at that moment Liam had shouted that the cake was being cut, and everyone had stampeded to the front of the room. When they came back, the teasing was simply gone. Nobody had challenged anybody. The distraction had eaten it.

She turned that into an inference: if teasing needs an audience and momentum, then breaking the momentum might work better than attacking the teaser. She decided to invest one try in testing it, today, at this table. If it failed, at least she'd know.

Braden leaned over Dex's tray. "Hey, spill king, you want a bib?"

Harper stood up fast and pointed at the window. "There's a hawk on the fence," she said, loud enough for the whole table. Heads swung. A big bird sat on the chain link by the portables, gray-brown, turning its head. Three kids got up to look, then five, then most of the table was crowded at the glass. Someone said it might be a Cooper's hawk, and an argument started about Cooper's hawks versus red-tails, and Dex came to the window too, milk forgotten.

By the time the hawk lifted off toward the track, lunch was nearly over and people were collecting trays. Braden got pulled into a debate about whether the bird was even real or just a pigeon. He never came back to the milk. On the way to fifth period, Dex fell into step beside Harper.

"Was there really a hawk?" he asked.

"There was," she said. "I just didn't expect it to matter."

"Next time," Dex said, "you could invest in something closer to the ground. I hear the fourth graders are releasing crickets in the gym on Friday."
