story:
Easton had forty minutes before Maya's parents got home, and the onion was winning. Every time he pressed the knife down, the cutting board skated three inches toward the edge of the counter like it was trying to escape.

"Stop moving," he told it.

"Boards don't listen," said Maya, who was browning garlic at the stove and had appointed herself head chef despite contributing mainly commentary. "Also you're holding the knife like it insulted you."

"I'm holding it exactly how the video said. Claw grip, fingertips tucked, knuckles forward." He curled his left hand over the half onion like a bear paw with a manicure. "The problem is the board, not me."

The board disagreed. He sliced, it skidded, and the onion chunk shot off the counter and landed near the dog bowl, where it would soon be found by a golden retriever who interpreted every dropped object as a gift. Easton retrieved it and considered the situation. The board slid every single time he pushed down, but it never slid when Maya stirred something on the far side. He stared at the counter, then at the thin wet ring the onion had left behind, then had an idea that felt almost too simple.

He wet a dish towel under the tap, wrung it out, and spread it flat under the board.

"Now you're just decorating," Maya said.

"Watch."

He set the knife down and pushed the board sideways with his palm. It didn't budge. He pushed harder. Nothing. It was as if the counter had decided to hold on.

"Huh," said Maya.

"That counts as a victory," Easton said, and got back to the onion. With the board finally sitting still, the claw grip actually worked, and thin half-moons of onion started stacking up in an orderly little pile instead of scattering like startled fish. He swept them into the pot with the garlic, where they hissed and softened. Maya crushed the canned tomatoes with her hands, which she claimed was authentic and he suspected was just fun.

"Technically an onion is a decomposer's dream," Maya said, sniffing the steam. "Humid in there, warm, full of sugar. Fungi would move in within a week."

"Then let's not give them a week."

They plated the pasta at 6:28, sauce still bubbling, two minutes to spare. When her parents walked in, her dad sniffed the air and said, "Something smells like an actual restaurant."

Maya pointed her fork at Easton. "He tamed the cutting board."

"It was the wet towel," Easton said, and went back for seconds.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
story:
Lydia slapped her pencil down on the climate graph and pointed at the tall blue bars. "No way this place is a rainforest. Look at October. The rain practically stops."

Marcus leaned over her shoulder, blocking the fluorescent light. "You're only looking at the bars. Check the line, the temperature one. That's the part that hinders your whole theory."

She traced the red line across the months with her finger. Every city on the worksheet had two graphs side by side, one for a desert and one for a rainforest, and their teacher had said only one thing before turning them loose: use the numbers, not the pictures. The room was warm and slightly humid from the radiator, whose valve had been dripping steam all week, and Lydia wiped her palms on her jeans before picking the pencil back up.

"Fine," she said. "October's line is at twenty-one degrees. And the bar shows... sixty-two millimeters." She wrote both numbers in the margin. November: twenty degrees, seventy millimeters. December: nineteen degrees, sixty-one. She worked down the whole year, month by month, while Marcus read the numbers out loud and she recorded them. Somewhere in July she started slowing down, hoping to find one month that would break the pattern, one month below eighteen degrees or under sixty millimeters of rain. There wasn't one.

"Ms. Okafor said this is the Koppen system," Marcus said, chewing his pen cap. "Every month over eighteen degrees and at least sixty millimeters of rain, and it counts as tropical rainforest."

"Then it counts," Lydia said quietly. She looked at the desert graph beside it, where the temperature line swung like a jump rope between blazing summer and freezing winter, and where half the bars were barely whiskers above zero. She had been so certain, so ready to argue in front of the class that the flat-looking graph was the dry one, that the truth landing on her desk felt like losing something.

She raised her hand anyway. "I want to change my answer. The second graph is the rainforest."

"Because of the rule, or because Marcus talked you into it?" Ms. Okafor asked from the front.

"Because of the rule." Lydia slid the paper forward, all twelve months tallied in the margin, and heard Marcus exhale beside her, half relieved and half like he'd already moved on to arguing with the next pair. The radiator hissed, and a drop of water fell from the valve onto her shoe.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
story:
Louis sat at his grandfather's kitchen table with a pencil, a ruler, and a blank page that seemed to be mocking him. His art teacher had assigned a drawing of a street, and he wanted it to look real, not like a flat cartoon road. He drew two lines that ran straight down the page, side by side, and frowned. It looked like a ladder lying on the ground.

He carried the paper out to the porch, where his grandfather was shelling peas. "What's wrong with it?" his grandfather asked.

"It doesn't look like it goes anywhere," Louis said. "It's just two lines."

His grandfather set down the bowl. "When I was about your age, I used to stand on the footbridge behind the church and watch the trains. My brother swore the rails got closer together far down the line. We nearly fell off that bridge arguing about it."

"Did they?" Louis asked.

"Go see for yourself."

Louis walked the dirt path to the footbridge and leaned over the rail. The two rails left the bridge beneath his feet, perfectly parallel, as wide apart as they always were. But down the line, a quarter mile away, they seemed to draw together, tighter and tighter, until they touched at some point he couldn't quite name. He stayed there a long time, watching, and an intuition took shape in him: the rails never actually moved, but they looked as if they met in the distance. His brother had been fooled by looking; his grandfather, he guessed, had been right.

Back at the table, Louis tried an experiment. He drew a dot in the middle of his page, then ran two lines from the bottom edges of the paper straight toward that dot, like the rails converging under the bridge. He added windows and doorways with their tops and bottoms angled toward the same spot. The street suddenly stretched away from him, deep and solid, as if he could walk down it. He erased the dot itself, since you couldn't see it in real life, and the drawing held anyway.

"Better," his grandfather said over his shoulder. "You've stopped being negligent about the far end of things."

"It's called a vanishing point," Louis said, tapping the spot with his pencil. "The rails look like they meet there, even though they never touch." He turned the page toward the window, checking his lines one more time, then wrote his name in the corner.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
story:
Hailey sat in the back corner of the computer lab, tapping her pencil against the desk while the projector hummed at the front of the room. Mr. Reyes had written one task on the board in green marker: write a program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime. She had typed the first two lines easily, n = int(input("Give me a number: ")), but after that her screen showed nothing but a blinking cursor, and the bell was twenty minutes away.

The problem circled in her head like a wasp. A prime number has no divisors except one and itself; she knew that part cold from math class. But how could a computer tell if a number divided evenly? When she did it by hand, she could see the answer come out with no remainder. The machine couldn't see anything. It just calculated.

Across the aisle, Deshawn was already testing his program, and the sound of his keys clicking made her jaw tighten. She leaned over. "How'd you do the dividing part?" she whispered. He turned his monitor toward her. "You don't divide, really. You use percent." She read his line: if n % d == 0. "Percent like percentage?" she asked. That seemed ambiguous, like it might mean something about ratios. "No, it's the remainder," Deshawn said. "In Python, percent gives you the remainder." She stared at the symbol, and the concept landed all at once, like a light snapping on in a dark hallway.

Her fingers started moving. She built a loop with d counting up from 2, and inside it she wrote the check: if n % d == 0, then n had a divisor that split it evenly, so it wasn't prime. She tried 9 first, and the program printed "not prime" because 9 % 3 came out to nothing left over. Then she tried 7, and every remainder showed up stubborn and lopsided, so it printed "prime." She smelled the dry, dusty warmth of the lab's old computers and grinned at her screen.

Then she typed 1, and the program said "prime," which she knew was wrong. She chewed her thumbnail. One wasn't a special mystery; her loop never even ran for it, because it started counting at 2. She added a quick check at the top: if n < 2, print "not prime." When she tested 2 and then 1 again, both answers came out right.

Mr. Reyes passed behind her and paused, reading over her shoulder. He didn't say anything at first, just tapped the edge of her desk twice and moved on. Deshawn raised his hand to ask about 1, and Hailey turned around in her seat. "I already fixed that one," she said. "Wanna race on 999,983?"

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
story:
Elizabeth turned the hose on low and aimed it at the mound of dirt she had spent an hour piling at the low end of the yard. The water slid down the slope in a thin ribbon, no wider than her thumb.

"That's it?" Marcus said from the fence. He was the neighbor's kid, and he had laughed when she told him what she was doing. "You said you were going to make a canyon. That little trickle couldn't carve anything. The Grand Canyon is a mile deep."

"It's not about one day." She nudged the hose a degree to the left. "The Little Colorado River isn't some giant, either. It just never stops."

Marcus climbed the fence and dropped into her yard. "So your hose is going to run for millions of years?"

"No. But I can speed everything else up." She had built the mound loose on purpose, half dirt and half sand, so the water could bite into it fast. In real rock, the same thing took ages. She had read about a Scottish geologist, James Hutton, who argued way back in 1785 that slow, everyday processes like erosion, working over immense time, shaped Earth's surface. No flood, no catastrophe. Just ordinary water, refusing to quit.

"You mean like a tenant who stays in a house so long the house wears out around him?" Marcus said.

"Sort of, except the river is the tenant and it never moves out." She let the water run. The ribbon found a groove, deepened it, collapsed a chunk of bank, and carried the sand downhill in a muddy cloud. At the base of the mound the water slowed, and the sand settled out in a small fan, building a flat delta an inch at a time. Deposition, right there on the grass. "See how it drops the sand when it slows? That's the other half. The river takes material from one place and dumps it in another."

They watched for twenty minutes. A trench opened down the middle of the mound, deep enough now that the water ran shadowed inside it, curling around a pebble that had become a boulder in the streambed's scale. Marcus crouched and pressed his finger into the fan of sand.

"Okay," he said. "So if a drip of water can do that in an afternoon, a river with a few million years." He didn't finish it. He put his hand into the current and dammed it. The water pooled behind his fingers, then spilled over the top and cut a new channel around his knuckle.

"Exactly," Elizabeth said. "It finds a way around everything. It's basically inevitable." She pulled his hand out, and the flood chewed the new channel twice as deep in under a minute.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
story:
The first time Alicia ran the eight hundred metres, she sprinted the first lap like a burglar fleeing a crime scene, then spent the second lap moving at a speed roughly equivalent to a shopping cart with a bad wheel. Coach Reyes timed her anyway, out of politeness. She collapsed on the infield grass and watched her shoelaces rotate slowly, like they were the ones who had run.

"There has to be a secret," she told Marcus, who was folding himself into a hamstring stretch nearby. Marcus wanted one thing in life, which was to beat his older brother's four-hundred time, and he talked about it so often that Alicia could recite it. Right now he was not thinking about the eight hundred at all.

"The secret is don't do it," Marcus said. "Eight hundred metres is the worst race. It's too long to sprint and too short to rest."

That night Alicia watched the 2012 London Olympic final, David Rudisha's world record run, on her mother's laptop. She timed the laps herself, thumb on her phone stopwatch. First lap, then second lap. She sat back. His first lap was more than two seconds faster than his second. The fastest man ever to run the distance had not run it evenly. He had spent more than he kept.

The next morning she told Marcus, who was doing starts in lane four whether anyone had asked him to or not.

"So even Rudisha went out fast," he said, "but not stupid fast."

"Two seconds isn't nothing," Alicia said. She had a theory now, which was that the first lap was a fire you had to light at exactly the right size, and the second lap was what happened when it burned down. Too big a fire and there was nothing left but smoke and apology.

At Thursday practice she tried it. First lap controlled, arms loose, breathing like she'd practiced in the hallway until her mother asked if she was okay. Coming off the final bend of lap one, her legs sent up their usual complaint, and she half expected them to fracture on the spot, though she knew that wasn't how fractures worked. She ignored the complaint. She had budgeted for it.

On the second lap she was still passing people. One of them was a girl from another school who said something unrepeatable, and Alicia found that very reassuring, actually.

At the line she was eight seconds faster than last week. She bent over, hands on knees, and checked her stopwatch twice in case the first reading was a lie.

"Three-oh-two," Marcus read over her shoulder. "That's two seconds off my brother's pace. For the four."

"Wrong race," Alicia said, still gasping.

"I know what race it is." He was already walking to the starting line, shaking out his arms. "Watch my start. Tell me if my first thirty metres look like yours."

story:
The blank document had been open for forty minutes, and the cursor blinked at Jayden like it was timing him. The essay was due Monday morning, and it had to be persuasive, with a real argument, and his teacher had said something about a thesis that he had half heard from the back row. He was at Grandpa's house for the weekend because Mom's work trip got prolonged by three days, and the Wi-Fi was so slow in the den that the page kept freezing.

"Still staring at nothing?" Grandpa asked, carrying two glasses of lemonade. He set one down next to the laptop and nodded at the screen.

"I don't know how to start," Jayden said. "I keep trying to write the first sentence and it's all garbage."

Grandpa pulled a battered shoebox from the shelf behind the desk. Inside were hundreds of index cards, soft with age, each one holding a single line in cramped pencil. "I never started with sentences," he said. "First I decided what I wanted to say. Then I worried about words." He tapped a card. "Thesis. That's the whole point of the thing, in one line." Then he laid three more cards on the desk in a row, side by side. "Three reasons under it. That's how I did every report for thirty years."

Jayden picked up the cards. Grandpa's handwriting was small and sure. Each card said only what it meant, not how it would sound. He grabbed a stack of fresh index cards from his backpack and wrote one word at the top of the first one: TREES. Then, without letting himself think about sentence style at all, he scribbled a single line: "The oak in Grandpa's yard should not be cut down." Under it he made three cards: shade, history, animal homes. His hand moved fast because nothing had to sound good yet.

He was halfway through filling in the third card when he noticed a yellow sheet stuck to the refrigerator through the doorway. It was a work order from a tree removal company, dated Friday. His stomach dropped. He walked over and picked it up, and his eyes went to the address line, which matched the house number on the mailbox outside. "Grandpa," he called, holding the paper up, his voice strange in his own ears. "This is your address. What's happening Friday?"

Grandpa came in drying his hands, read the sheet, and sighed. "Council says the roots are cracking the sewer line. I didn't want to tell you before your visit."

Jayden looked from the work order to his three cards lying in a row on the desk. "Then my essay isn't practice anymore," he said slowly, an idea forming. "Grandpa, do you have a copy machine?"

"Down the hall, under the coupon drawer."

Jayden gathered his cards and headed for the hallway. "The parks office is open Monday, and I'm going to make sure this is on top of the stack."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
story:
Lauren stood in the kitchen doorway with the reading folded in her hand, watching her grandmother press dough flat with the heel of her palm. Her grandmother pressed slowly, the way she did everything since the doctors said the cartilage in her knees was wearing thin, and Lauren felt a flash of guilt for even asking.

"Abuela, did you have a quinceañera?"

"I did. In Guadalajara." Her grandmother dusted flour from her fingers. "It started at church. It always starts that way, mija. A Mass of thanksgiving, first thing, before any dancing."

Lauren's stomach dropped. She had been planning for the party, the dress, the waltz. Now her mother was telling her that in three weeks, at the beginning of the Mass, she would stand in front of everyone and deliver a reading from memory. In Spanish. She had tried learning it silently on her bed for two nights, and every time she got to the fourth line, the words deteriorated into a jumble, like wet sand slipping through her fingers.

"Abuela, how did you memorize things? For school?" She was guessing her grandmother had a method, some hidden trick she had never been taught. Her grandmother laughed and tapped her own ear.

"I couldn't read then, not well. I learned everything by hearing it. My mother would say a line, and I would say it back, out loud, until my brothers begged me to stop."

Lauren tested the idea that same afternoon. She recorded herself reading the passage on her phone, then played it in a loop while she swept the porch, saying each line out loud right after her own recorded voice. By dinner she had eight lines solid. Out loud worked. Silent staring did not. There was a rule hiding in that, she was sure, something about the ears being a legitimate second memory, a door the eyes couldn't open.

The twist came on Sunday. Her mother sat beside her at the kitchen table and picked up the paper. "We should practice," she said, but her voice was strange, thin, and she turned the page sideways as if admiring the margins.

"You're nervous," Lauren said.

"Spanish Mass readings were never my thing." Her mother's cheeks went pink. "I was going to quietly hand the paper to the lector and let him read it for you."

Lauren stared. All week her mother had been drilling her, timing her, and now it turned out her mother had been ready to let the whole thing slide? Then Lauren slid the phone across the table, pressed play, and said, "Then you learn it my way. Line by line, out loud. You say it, I say it back."

Her mother pressed record, took a breath, and began.

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
story:
Norah balanced her backpack on her knees as the bus rattled past the hardware store, trying to read the wrinkled handout without letting it touch the sticky seat. Mrs. Okafor had assigned the balcony scene from Romeo and Juliet, and by tomorrow each pair had to paraphrase every speech into modern English and perform it in front of the class. Norah's stomach dropped every time she thought about standing up there, so she figured she would at least get the words right.

The trouble was that the words made no sense. She read Juliet's line again. "O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?" She scribbled underneath: Romeo, Romeo, where are you, Romeo? That seemed obvious. Juliet was on the balcony, Romeo was hiding in the garden, so of course she was asking where he was.

Deshaun slid into the seat across the aisle, his own copy folded into a paper airplane. He saw her pencil hovering and leaned over. "You stuck already?"

"Juliet's looking for him," Norah said. "She wants to know where he is."

Deshaun unfolded his page and ran his finger down to a note in the margin, one Mrs. Okafor had circled in red. He read it, then looked up with a grin that made Norah suspicious. "She's not asking where. Wherefore means why."

"Why?"

"Yes. Why. Like, why do you have to be Romeo?" He tapped the next lines, where Juliet begs him to deny his name. "She just found out the guy she likes is a Montague, and her family hates Montagues. So she's going, why him, of all people? Why did I have to fall for the one boy I can't have?"

Norah stared at her own paraphrase, where are you, Romeo, and felt her ears go hot. "That completely changes it," she said slowly. "She's not searching the garden. She's arguing with the universe."

Deshaun laughed. "Arguing with the universe. That's good. Write that down."

She crossed out her line and started over. Why do you have to be Romeo? Take the name off and be somebody else. Then a thought hit her, and she sat up straight. "Wait. This is the whole scene. She's saying the name is the problem, not the person. He could just... not be Romeo." She tested it against the rest of the speech, and it held. Every line was about names, about what you inherit from your family whether you want it or not. Her family had inherited her grandmother's house, and nobody had asked Norah's opinion about the ugly green kitchen either.

"I get it now," she said, and copied the new version in her best handwriting.

Deshaun pulled out a granola bar, broke it in half, and handed her the bigger piece. "You look kind of shaky," he said. "Sugar helps. So does knowing your stuff, and you know it."

"Mostly I'm scared of messing up in front of everyone," Norah admitted, taking the piece. "I feel like the second I stand up, I'm completely vulnerable."

"Then don't stand up," Deshaun said. "We'll sit. Downstage, whatever that means. Mrs. Okafor never said we had to stand."

Norah looked at him. "You'd really do the scene sitting down?"

"I'd do it lying on the floor if it helps you talk." He took a bite of his half. "Besides, I still have to paraphrase my whole speech, and you're the only one on this bus who knows wherefore means why."

"Deal," Norah said, and handed him her pencil.

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
story:
Sawyer pressed the multimeter probes against the fat copper wire and squinted at the screen. The exhibit card said "Measure It Yourself," and it wasn't kidding: two wires sat side by side on the table, a thick one and a spaghetti-thin one, both hooked to batteries. His little sister Priya wanted to move on to the static electricity ball, but Sawyer had a plan. He was going to figure out the resistance of each wire all by himself, the way a real engineer would.

First he measured voltage, which meant clipping the probes across each wire while the battery pushed current through it. Then he clipped the meter in line with the wire to read the current. He wrote both numbers on the back of his ticket stub. "Voltage divided by current," he muttered. "That gives resistance." The thick wire read 6 volts and 2 amps, which worked out to 3 ohms. Easy.

The thin wire gave him trouble. He measured it twice because the current looked wrong somehow, too small, and he was starting to feel pessimistic about his whole method. Maybe the battery was dying. Maybe he had clipped something backward. He checked everything, then did the math anyway: 6 volts, 0.5 amps. He frowned at the stub. "Twelve ohms? That's four times the thick one. Same battery, same length. How can one wire be that much harder to push through?"

Priya leaned over his shoulder. "Maybe the skinny one's just worse," she said.

"But why would it be worse?" Sawyer turned the thin wire in his fingers. It was the same copper, the same silvery shine, the same length coiled beside its partner. Nothing he could see was different except the size. And you couldn't see resistance at all. It was like guessing what was inside a wrapped present from how heavy it felt. He wondered if that was the whole answer hiding in plain sight. He pulled a volunteer's clipboard toward him and sketched two circles, one wide, one narrow. "If current is like a crowd trying to get through a hallway," he said slowly, "a fat hallway is easy and a skinny one is a traffic jam."

He had to revise his ticket-stub notes now, because he'd labeled the wires A and B in the wrong order. He crossed them out and rewrote: thick, 3 ohms; thin, 12 ohms. When the museum lights flickered for the four o'clock show in the planetarium, Priya tugged his sleeve, but Sawyer grabbed one more reading first, probes steady, eyes fixed on the little screen. "Just once more," he said. "Science."

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
story:
Hunter had exactly one hour to learn how to order lunch in Spanish before his Spanish club walked to the little restaurant on Maple Street for their end-of-term practice session. He sat at a desk in the back of Mrs. Alvarez's empty classroom, hunched over a menu she had photocopied for him, converting English phrases in his head into the new words he'd memorized that week: el sándwich, la sopa, ¿cuánto cuesta? He could ask how much it cost. He could name the food. What he couldn't figure out was why Mrs. Alvarez kept writing "para llevar" in the margins of his practice sheet, next to every order he'd drafted.

His real problem was bigger than the assignment. His bus left at 3:15 for his brother's soccer tournament, and the club's lunch reservation was at 2:30. If he wanted to eat anything, it would have to be on the bus, wrapped up, not on a plate at a table. He had no idea how to say that.

He tried a test. He asked his friend Daisy, who sat two rows over working on her own menu, "What do people say when they want the food to go? Like, wrapped up, not eaten there?"

Daisy shrugged. "Beats me. I'm just ordering the soup and staying put."

So Hunter hunted through the photocopied menu. Near the bottom, in small print, he found a line: "Precios para llevar: $4.50." The takeout prices, Mrs. Alvarez had said, were cheaper than the sit-down ones. That meant "para llevar" had something to do with taking food away instead of eating it there. He wasn't sure, but it was the only pattern he could find, and it showed up next to every boxed-meal price on the page.

At the restaurant, the smell of toasted bread drifted under the canopy of faded umbrellas out front. Hunter got in line behind his classmates, watching them order one by one. When his turn came, the man at the counter waited, pencil ready.

"Un sándwich de pollo, por favor," Hunter said. Then he pointed at the wrapped sandwiches in the glass case and took his best shot. "Para llevar."

The man's pencil paused, then he nodded and reached into the case instead of toward the plates stacked behind him. He wrapped the sandwich in white paper and slid it across the counter.

"Cuesta cuatro cincuenta," the man said, and Hunter recognized the number from the menu's small print, the cheaper takeout price. He counted out the bills, gripping the warm package. It had worked. He had guessed the rule from the prices, and the man's nod had proved it.

He jogged out to the bus stop with the sandwich tucked under his arm, tearing one corner of the paper as he climbed the steps. His classmates, still settling their plates back at the restaurant, would eat slowly under the umbrellas, but he would eat too, somewhere past Maple Street, on the road toward the game. He took a bite and grinned at the window. "Para llevar," he said to his reflection, and the bus rumbled forward.

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
story:
The essay prompt sat on Zack's desk like a dare: should the town keep its old movie theater or sell it for a parking lot? He had strong feelings, but when he tried to start writing, his page stayed barren except for his name. He had two pages due Friday, and it was already Wednesday study hall in the library, where the radiators ticked and dust hung in the slanted light near the window.

His friend Priya slid into the chair across from him with a stack of books and a granola bar. "Stuck?"

"I know what I think," Zack said. "I just can't get it to make sense on paper. And my thoughts keep running into each other."

Priya tapped his blank page. "So don't write the essay yet. Write one sentence that says what you think and why. One sentence, three reasons."

Zack stared at the window, where a crow was walking the ledge. He tried it out loud. "The town should keep the theater because it brings people downtown, it's the cheapest thing for families to do, and it's the only old building left on Main Street."

"That's a thesis," Priya said. "Now make each reason its own paragraph."

"Paragraphs already? I haven't written anything."

She pulled his paper toward her and folded it into rough columns with her finger. "Watch. Give me three reasons and a made-up first sentence for each one."

He tried the first. "The theater gets people to come downtown, because on census weekends the diner says it's full after the late show."

"Okay. Now say how it connects back."

He tried again, slower, testing the idea the way he'd test a stick on thin ice. "Because bringing people downtown is one reason to keep the theater." It felt almost too simple. He wrote it down anyway.

Priya leaned over and read only the first line of each paragraph he drafted, skipping everything else, humming to show she wasn't peeking. Then she sat back. "Keep the theater, downtown business, cheap family nights, last old building. I got your whole argument without reading a word in between."

Zack looked at his paper, surprised. "Just from the openers?"

"Every paragraph starts with its own topic sentence," Priya said, "and the topic sentence hooks that point back to your thesis. So I could follow it like a trail of bread crumbs."

He read his three opening lines again, then crossed out one and wrote a sharper version, because now he could hear where his own argument wobbled. The page was filling up, column by column, and the crow on the ledge lifted off into the gray afternoon.

"One more paragraph," he said, and clicked his pen.
